content: In an effort to enhance integration across various health services, the World Health Organization (WHO) is preparing to release a Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) for family planning. Additionally, a DAK for postnatal care (PNC) is being developed and will be released following the publication of the PNC guidelines. These efforts aim to ensure continuity of care across the sexual and reproductive health spectrum, alongside DAKs for other health domains. Scenario 1: Incorporating WHO Guidelines into Existing Digital Systems Countries with existing digital systems, such as electronic medical records (EMRs) and decision-support tools, can utilize the DAK to verify alignment of their health program content and data—such as antenatal care (ANC) or family planning—with WHO guidelines. Users can extract specific decision algorithms from the DAK to integrate into their systems. By systematically reviewing this documentation, health program managers and implementers can identify discrepancies in workflows, data inputs, and decision-support logic. This process helps them understand the rationale for deviations and adapt guideline content to local contexts. Scenario 2: Transitioning from Paper-Based to Digital Systems Countries currently using paper-based systems may find the process of digitizing client-level records and decision-support systems daunting. The DAK serves as a starting point to streamline necessary data elements and decision-support logic for optimized digital systems. Users can cross-reference paper-based tools to identify missing fields or content that should be included in the digital system. Additionally, the WHO Handbook for digitizing primary health care provides stepwise guidance on mapping paper-based data into digital systems, addressing redundant or non-value-adding data elements. Scenario 3: Linking Aggregate and Individual-Level Data In some cases, countries may have digital systems for aggregate reporting and health management information systems (HMIS) but lack digital systems at the service-delivery level (e.g., community or facility level). The DAK includes aggregate indicators derived from individual-level data to bridge these levels. Complementary guidance, such as the Analysis and use of facility data for RMNCAH program managers, should also be consulted to support the use of routine data at facility and district levels. Scenario 4: Promoting Interoperability and Integrated Systems The DAK includes data elements mapped to standards such as ICD codes to facilitate the design of interoperable systems. The data dictionary in the Web Annex provides necessary codes for various data elements, reducing the time required for implementers to incorporate global standards into their digital systems. Scenario 5: Adapting the WHO ANC Digital Module WHO will release a reference ANC digital module as a decision-support and digital tracking tool, reflecting the ANC DAK content. This module will help countries identify which data elements and decision-support logic need modification for their specific contexts. Engaging with clients, such as pregnant women, is a critical component of service delivery. Emerging approaches include transmitting health information and reminders, enabling clients to access their medical records, and supporting self-monitoring of health and diagnostic data. The content requirements for these client-facing tools will be detailed in a forthcoming self-care interventions DAK. Assumptions Underlying the Use of the ANC DAK The use of the ANC DAK is based on several assumptions: The woman’s pregnancy is confirmed, and she intends to proceed with it. ANC services are provided as part of routine primary care, not specialized services. Local adaptations will be made to the DAK, as it is designed to reflect commonalities across settings (80% generic content, 20% localized content). National policymakers have adopted or plan to adopt WHO ANC guidelines for a positive pregnancy experience. For countries yet to adopt the 2016 WHO ANC guideline, the DAK can support the transition by presenting recommended interventions in a digitizable format. Linkages to the Broader Digital Health Ecosystem DAKs are part of the broader digital health ecosystem and should be used within a strategic vision for digital tracking and decision-support (DTDS) systems. In contexts lacking such a vision, users should first consult resources like the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit and WHO guidelines on digital interventions for health system strengthening to better understand how to select and apply appropriate digital health interventions. Health Interventions and Recommendations in the ANC DAK The ANC DAK focuses on key health interventions defined in the WHO Universal Health Coverage (UHC) compendium, including: Health education and counseling to promote healthy pregnancy. Nutritional supplementation during pregnancy. Maternal and fetal assessment and screening. Preventive measures and vaccination during pregnancy. Treatment for physiological symptoms during pregnancy. ANC models with a minimum of eight contacts. The DAK reflects health recommendations already published in WHO guidelines and guidance documents. It also incorporates systematic screening for tuberculosis, diagnostic criteria for hyperglycemia in pregnancy, and recommendations for community mobilization, among others. Personas in the ANC DAK Personas represent relevant stakeholders or end-users of the system. While specific roles and demographics vary by setting, generic personas are based on WHO core competencies for health workers. These personas are developed as a starting point and require further contextualization to address the needs, motivations, and challenges of targeted users in each setting. Skilled healthcare professionals in primary care settings are the primary personas for the ANC DAK. These professionals are defined as competent maternal and newborn health providers trained to national and international standards, capable of delivering evidence-based, human-rights-based, and culturally sensitive care. They are also equipped to manage physiological processes during labor and delivery and to identify, manage, or refer complications.
